title: Teaching

title: Teaching
text:
Teaching philosophy
I want students to think critically, solve practical problems and understand statistical ideas deeply. My classes combine theory with real-world applications through R, R Shiny apps, live coding and group work, in an environment where every student feels able to take part.
I adapt my approach to each audience. For service courses I simplify concepts without losing depth, I take applied students through both the theory and the software, and I give mathematically strong students harder problems.
Innovations I have introduced include:

Posit (RStudio) Cloud for real-time feedback on students’ scripts during online learning
R Shiny applications that let students explore statistical concepts without prior coding experience
A pre-semester R bootcamp (2022) to close gaps left by online learning
Group R Shiny projects for applied, collaborative learning
Sentiment analysis of students’ written feedback to better understand their learning experience

title: Join
text:
Prospective students


Honours

I supervise Honours projects every year, usually on one of my core themes: spatio-stochastic modelling, spatial epidemiology, wastewater surveillance or tuberculosis modelling. A strong foundation in statistics and an interest in R are a good start.



Masters

I am happy to supervise Masters students on topics that fit my research programme. Please send a short research statement and your academic transcript.



PhD

I currently supervise one PhD student and welcome enquiries from candidates interested in spatial epidemiology or statistical public health, particularly as new funding becomes available.

title: Research funding
text:
About my funding
My early research was funded through collaborative partnerships within SEPIMOD, where I developed spatial and computational models and contributed modelling and data analysis expertise to national COVID-19 and wastewater surveillance work.
I now lead independently funded research. The NRF Thuthuka grant supports statistical methods for spatially misaligned health data, spatio-temporal models for disease surveillance and spatial optimisation tools for tuberculosis interventions. A new IMSA and Investec grant extends this work to non-communicable diseases.

title: Dr Raeesa Manjoo-Docrat
text:
Statistics · Spatial epidemiology




Lecturer, School of Statistics and Actuarial Science, University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg


Email Google Scholar ORCID ResearchGate LinkedIn
I have been a Lecturer in Statistics at the University of the Witwatersrand since 2018. My work centres on spatio-stochastic models that capture the spatially uneven way epidemics spread, with applications to COVID-19, tuberculosis and wastewater-based disease surveillance. I completed a postdoctoral fellowship in tuberculosis modelling at Johns Hopkins University in 2024.
I am a founding member of the SEPIMOD COVID-19 modelling consortium, which brings together Wits, the University of Pretoria, the CSIR and the South African Medical Research Council, and of the Old Mutual–Wits Risk Lab. I also coordinate mentoring for STEM MentHer and care a great deal about helping students move from Honours into research careers.

title: Dr Raeesa Manjoo-Docrat
text:
Research



Spatio-stochastic models of disease spread
Discrete-time binomial chain models with spatial structure, capturing local transmission, interaction between regions and movement between spatial units.




Spatial epidemiology of COVID-19
Spatially explicit, age-stratified SEIR models that combine mobility data with a vulnerability index reflecting socioeconomic and health disparities, to guide targeted public health responses.




Wastewater-based surveillance
Low-cost, community-level surveillance from wastewater, including methods for spatially misaligned data, early warning and hotspot detection in urban and peri-urban settings.




Tuberculosis in vulnerable populations
Individual-based models of TB in high-risk groups, the effect of COVID-19 disruptions on TB epidemiology, and spatial optimisation of vaccination and resource allocation.




Non-communicable diseases
Spatio-temporal analysis of non-communicable diseases, a new programme funded by IMSA and Investec (2026–2029).




Teaching statistics with R
Evaluating how R is taught across undergraduate and postgraduate curricula, and building open-source tools for spatial epidemiological modelling.
